claims.text: Lattice distortions caused by atomic size mismatch are the primary control on strength and deformation or failure behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Atomic size mismatch generates local stress fields.
The local stress fields generated by lattice distortion impede dislocation motion.
Lattice-distortion stress fields impede dislocation motion more effectively than other microstructural factors when grain-boundary contributions are held constant.
Changing alloying-element combinations can systematically vary atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions can be measured using high-resolution diffraction or electron-microscopy strain mapping.
Increased atomic size mismatch introduces increased local lattice strain.
Local lattice strains act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion suppresses plastic deformation and enhances yield strength.
Increased atomic size mismatch alters failure modes.
Samples with higher atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than baseline samples with lower atomic size mismatch.
Samples with higher atomic size mismatch will exhibit different strain-hardening or fracture behavior than samples with lower mismatch.
Minimizing atomic size mismatch reduces lattice distortion.
Low-mismatch baseline alloys are expected to have lower yield strength.
The proposed relationship should hold in single-phase concentrated alloys with minimized grain-boundary contributions and dislocation-controlled deformation.
The proposed relationship is not expected to govern when thermal activation or phase transformations control deformation.
Failure to observe a statistically significant strength increase or a distinctive deformation or failure response in the high-mismatch samples would falsify the dominance hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions require grain-boundary effects to be minimized, whereas the baseline is described as having deformation behavior dominated by grain-boundary effects. The latter would undermine the intended isolation of lattice distortion.

The initial-state field permits samples with merely similar overall compositions, while the intervention says overall composition will be kept constant despite changing alloying-element combinations. It is unclear how elemental combinations can change while composition remains constant.
